turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if he had any other residences or connections in more reputable parts of London.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he had no other residences or connections in more reputable parts of London, only a small country residence in Hertfordshire.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if he was aware that a gentleman's residence in London was essential to his reputation and standing in society.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained to Lady Bracknell that he understood the importance of a gentleman having a London residence but his current situation was limited to his country residence.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted to Jack that without a proper London address, his social standing would be severely compromised and his future prospects dimmed.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained to Lady Bracknell that he was fully aware of the social importance of a London residence but his current circumstances did not permit such an establishment.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted to Jack that without a proper London residence, his social standing would be severely compromised and his future prospects dimmed. She added that such a residence was not a matter of choice but an absolute necessity for any gentleman aspiring to marry into the upper echelons of society.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he understood her concerns and that he was actively seeking to acquire a residence in London to meet the expectations of his social class and to better his prospects for marriage.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that her concerns were not merely about a London residence, but also about his background and character. She asked him to elucidate his origins, for a gentleman must be of impeccable lineage and reputation.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he was born in the handbag of a London taxicab and had been adopted by the late Mr Thomas Cardew, who was the guardian of Jack’s childhood friend, Cecily.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted to Jack that the circumstances of his birth were indeed most peculiar and quite unsuitable for a gentleman of his aspirations. She asked him to provide more details about his adoptive father, Mr Thomas Cardew, and his family connections.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that Mr Thomas Cardew was a respectable gentleman who had left him a substantial estate in the country, providing him with the means to support a family.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted to Jack that while the late Mr Thomas Cardew had indeed been a respectable gentleman, his family connections were not as illustrious as might be required for a gentleman of Jack’s current position in society.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he understood her concerns and wished to reassure her that his intentions were honourable and that he was committed to becoming a gentleman of the highest moral standards.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted to Jack that while she appreciated his earnestness, the matter of his birth and early years would remain a significant obstacle to his social advancement and suitability as a husband for Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she could not understand why such trivial matters as one’s birth should be allowed to interfere with one’s chance of happiness.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted to Gwendolen that in her world, the stability and respectability of one’s background were not trivial matters but the bedrock upon which a successful marriage and a prosperous future were built.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she refused to accept that a person’s worth was determined by their birth or social standing, and that she loved Jack for who he was and the man he aspired to be.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted to Gwendolen that her refusal to consider the importance of social standing and one’s origins was not a pragmatic approach to marriage and life’s challenges.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she would not let societal expectations dictate her happiness and that she intended to marry Jack regardless of his background.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen that she was not engaged to anyone and that when she did become engaged, she or her father would inform her of the fact.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell, 'Mamma!'

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to go to the carriage.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to get into the carriage.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he preferred standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she felt bound to inform him that he was not down on her list of eligible young men.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he must admit he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was glad to hear it and that a man should always have an occupation of some kind.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if he knew everything or nothing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was pleased to hear it and that she did not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if his income was in land or in investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that his income was in investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that it was satisfactory.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that a country house was satisfactory and asked how many bedrooms it had.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she did not know Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that Lady Bloxham went about very little and was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that nowadays that was no guarantee of respectability of character and asked what number in Belgrave Square.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that the number was 149.
